lessons.title: The farm supervisor's role in planning and control
lessons.html:
From doing the work to running the work

The National Certificate: Farming at NQF 4 is aimed at the person who stands between the farm manager and the field team: the foreman, the section supervisor, the young farmer taking over a block of the farm. At this level you are no longer only doing the tasks. You are expected to monitor, co-ordinate, plan and control the agricultural processes for one commodity, whether that is maize under dryland, citrus under drip, a broiler house or a beef herd on veld.

The four management functions on a farm

  • Plan: decide what must happen, when and with what. Example: a planting plan for 120 ha of soya beans that sets dates, seed rate, fertiliser, labour and tractor hours.
  • Organise: get people, equipment and inputs in place. Book the planter, service it, make sure the seed is on the farm a week before planting.
  • Lead and co-ordinate: brief the team each morning, give clear instructions, solve conflicts, keep sections working together.
  • Control: compare what happened with what was planned and act on the gaps. If only 80 ha was planted by the target date, find out why and fix it.

Choosing your commodity focus

The qualification lets you specialise in agronomy (field crops such as maize, wheat, sugarcane), horticulture (fruit, vegetables, nursery plants) or animal husbandry (cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, poultry). The management principles are the same, but the production calendar differs. A citrus supervisor plans around flowering, fruit set and the export packing season. A sheep supervisor plans around mating, lambing, shearing and marketing.

Decisions grounded in knowledge

Good supervisors base decisions on three kinds of knowledge: production knowledge (soil, plant or animal science), management knowledge (budgets, records, planning) and people knowledge (labour law, motivation, safety). A decision to irrigate, to vaccinate, or to move a team to another block should always be checked against all three: is it technically right, can we afford it, and do we have the right people to do it safely?

lessons.title: Records, budgets and people
lessons.html:
Controlling production with records

You cannot control what you do not measure. On a farm, records are the supervisor's main control tool. Typical records include:

AreaExample records
CropsPlanting dates, rainfall, spray records, yields per land
LivestockBirths, deaths, weights, treatments, stock counts per camp
LabourAttendance, hours, tasks completed, training
InputsStock of seed, fertiliser, chemicals, diesel

Compare records with your plan every week. A rising diesel use per hectare, a drop in calving percentage or many sick days in one team are early warnings.

Working with a budget

The farm manager usually sets the budget, but the supervisor spends much of it. Know your cost centres: if fertiliser for your section is budgeted at R450 000 and you have already spent R400 000 before top-dressing, report it early. Small savings matter: fixing a leaking irrigation line, reducing tractor idling, or cutting feed waste at the troughs.

Managing people fairly and safely

As a supervisor you represent the employer. You must follow the Basic Conditions of Employment Act and the sectoral determination for farm workers on working hours and pay, and the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 on safe work. In practice that means:

  • Clear daily instructions and realistic targets.
  • Correct protective clothing for spraying, chainsaw or workshop work.
  • Fair, consistent discipline that follows the farm's disciplinary code.
  • Training new workers before they use machinery or chemicals.

Continuous improvement

At the end of each season, sit with your manager and review: what went well, what went wrong, what should change next year. Write it down. This habit turns experience into better plans.

Key points

  • The NQF 4 farming supervisor plans, organises, leads and controls production for one commodity.
  • Decisions must be technically sound, affordable and safe for people.
  • Records are the main control tool: compare actual results with the plan every week.
  • Know your section's budget and report overspending early.
  • Follow labour law and the OHS Act 85 of 1993 in daily supervision.
